AI Method Note
How AI was used to complete the T01 assignment (Document Analysis and Organizational Synthesis) — Managing with Artificial Intelligence.
Tool. Claude Code (Anthropic) was used interactively across five sessions, one per task. It read the 31 source PDFs, wrote and ran its own Python scripts (extraction, tagging, TF-IDF, network analysis, charts) and assembled each report; every output was reviewed and corrected before moving on. Pattern: instruction → agent proposes/executes → shows figures/tables/page previews → I approve or request a change.
Mid-way check. Once the reports were fragmenting into more detail, I asked the agent to explain everything done so far in plain language, to confirm the direction before approving Task 4. Wrap-up: asked it to package all five reports into one ZIP for submission, then verified its contents.
Division of labour. The agent did the mechanical work (parsing, tagging, statistics, charts, layout) and proposed the analytical framing (the divergence axes, the blueprint layers). I set the direction at each step, checked outputs against the source PDFs, and pushed back when something looked over-claimed, too dense, or too long.
Stage | What I asked the agent | What the agent did | My check / correction
Kick-off | Shared the assignment and the 31-PDF archive; asked it to read the brief and propose how to tackle the five tasks. | Proposed a task-by-task plan (T1–T5), one report per task, and asked which language/format to use. | Confirmed: English, PDF, start with Task 1.
T1 Inventory | Automated metadata extraction (titles, authors, journals, dates, keywords) plus snippets; set the domain boundaries. | Built a pdfinfo/pdftotext pipeline, a 12-tag coverage scheme, TF-IDF terms, five charts, a full report. | Checked metadata against the PDFs (several had missing/wrong embedded fields); asked for TF-IDF noise, venue-count and wording fixes.
T2 Mapping | Build a topic tree and a cross-reference network from the T1 tags; flagged that reports shouldn't all be as long as T1. | Built a primary-method tree and a shared-tag network (NetworkX centrality/communities), reusing T1 data only. | First network was too dense to read → asked to raise the edge threshold; approved the shorter, 4-page version.
T3 Divergence | Wanted a deeper contrast of sub-topics and trade-offs, not another grouping. | Defined four divergence axes (guarantee vs. adaptivity, energy vs. time framing, 5 uncertainty philosophies, autonomy vs. explainability) with positioning charts. | Asked it to label clearly what was measured (tags) vs. judgment-based scoring, so charts weren't over-claimed.
T4 Synthesis | Wanted a unified blueprint (DRL + digital twin + XAI) under real metallurgical constraints, not a generic architecture. | Proposed a 5-layer architecture, each layer traced to specific source papers, plus concrete metallurgical constraints. | Verified every layer was grounded in a cited paper, and that open risks (sim-to-real gap, data readiness) were stated honestly.
T5 Briefing | Final report in AIDA format for a leadership audience; keep it short. | 2-page Attention–Interest–Desire–Action briefing with a phased roll-out and a clear decision ask. | Requested it stay to two pages and lead with the business decision, not technical detail.

Task 1 — Inventory & Initial Scan
Managing with Artificial Intelligence · T01 Class Assignment · Document Analysis and Organizational
Synthesis
Knowledge domain: AI-enabled, energy-efficient scheduling in steelmaking & furnace operations
1. Executive summary
The document set left behind by our former engineer contains 31 scientific documents (456 pages, ≈308k
words of body text) spread over 29 different venues and published between 2016 and 2026. No index,
reading notes or classification accompanied the archive, and the documents' own embedded metadata proved
unreliable: only 12 of 31 PDFs carry complete title/author/keyword fields. We therefore built a reproducible
extraction pipeline and a verified inventory ( T1_inventory.csv ) that becomes the backbone for Tasks 2–5.

Key findings of the initial scan
The domain has a clear core: scheduling of energy-intensive thermal assets (reheating and heat-
treatment furnaces, hot rolling, steelmaking–casting, ladles, by-product gas networks) under real
plant constraints.
The toolbox is shifting. Up to 2022, 10 of 14 documents relied on metaheuristics and only 1 used
reinforcement learning; since 2023, 5 of 17 use DRL, 4 digital twins and 4 explainability.
Knowledge is fragmented. No single document combines DRL, digital twins and XAI, and none of
the 5 XAI documents deals with a steel process. The trustworthy-AI knowledge sits apart from
the metallurgical knowledge.
Visible boundaries/gaps: CO₂ is only used as motivation (never as an optimisation objective), and
nothing covers predictive maintenance, economic business cases or organisational change
management.
2. Scope and method
Objective. Perform automated extraction of metadata (titles, authors, journals, dates, keywords) and initial
snippets, and use it to set the boundaries of the knowledge domain before mapping it (Task 2).
2.1 Extraction pipeline
1. Unpacking & embedded metadata — unzip  + pdfinfo  (Title, Author, Subject, Keywords, page
count).
2. Full-text extraction — pdftotext  (layout and first-page versions), reference lists and repeated running
headers removed.
3. Pattern-based parsing — regular expressions for DOIs, venue lines, keyword blocks and abstracts on
page 1.

4. Human-in-the-loop verification — every record checked against page 1 of the PDF; missing fields
completed and one-sentence snippets condensed from each abstract.
5. Automated term profile — TF-IDF (uni- and bi-grams, body text, author names and boilerplate
removed) giving 6 distinctive terms per document, a check that doesn't depend on the authors' own
keywords.
6. Coverage tagging — 12-tag scheme (context, objective and AI technique) applied to every document; it
becomes the seed of the Task 2 topic tree.
2.2 Tools we bring to the problem
An AI coding agent (Claude Code) to orchestrate the pipeline and draft the syntheses; open-source text tooling
(poppler pdfinfo/pdftotext ); Python ( pandas , scikit-learn  TF-IDF, matplotlib ); and the analyst's
judgement to validate every extracted record. All steps are scripted ( scripts/ ), so the inventory can be
regenerated when the archive grows.
2.3 Data-quality issues detected
Extraction itself shows the archive is fragmented. These issues would silently corrupt a purely automated
inventory:
Issue Extent Example / treatment
Embedded PDF metadata
missing or incomplete
8 none · 11 partial · 12 full Titles/authors recovered from page-1 text.
Wrong author in metadata 1 P13: the PDF lists the proceedings editor, not the four Fraunhofer authors.
Obfuscated font encoding 1 P13: DOI shifted by a character offset in the text layer; decoded to
10.15488/12158.
Duplicated text layers 1 P01 (IFAC): title/authors repeated 4× in extraction; text re-extracted in raw
mode.
No author keywords 1 P26: keywords derived from abstract (flagged as derived).
Online vs. issue year and in-
press status
5 P03, P05, P09, P10, P17 published online one or two years before the
issue; P29 still a corrected proof. Issue year used consistently.
Non-descriptive file names most Truncated names (e.g. “Assessing the Transparency and.pdf”,
“sustainability-13-09277-v3.pdf”). Stable IDs P01–P31 assigned.

3. Corpus overview
Figure 1. Documents per publication year and type (issue year).
The set is recent and speeds up after 2022: 17 documents (55%) are from 2023–2026, and 3 are from 2026.
The collection reflects an active research front, not a settled one.
Figure 2. Country of the lead affiliation.
Chinese groups lead 16 of 31 documents, mostly with plant data from Chinese mills. Europe (Germany, Austria,
Czechia, Italy, UK) contributes most of the DRL-for-energy, XAI and human-centric work. Brazil adds two
ArcelorMittal-related studies.

Figure 3. Most frequent author keywords (normalised synonyms, ≥2 occurrences).
Author keywords are highly dispersed: out of 151 keyword strings (122 distinct), only 14 concepts appear twice
or more. Authors describe overlapping problems with different vocabularies (“reheating furnace”, “heating
furnace”, “walking beam reheating furnace”, “soaking”). Topics therefore have to be detected from content (tags
and TF-IDF), not from keywords alone. Task 2 does this.

4. Inventory
The complete record (authors, DOI, keywords, TF-IDF terms, tags, snippet, file name) is in T1_inventory.csv

5. Initial content scan and domain boundaries
5.1 Coverage by tag
Tag Meaning All (31) 2016–22 (14) 2023–26 (17)
STEEL Steel / metals industry context 21 11 (79%) 10 (59%)
ENERGY Energy consumption or cost objective 18 10 (71%) 8 (47%)
UNC Uncertainty, robustness or dynamic rescheduling 11 5 (36%) 6 (35%)
EXACT Exact / mathematical programming (MILP, Benders, optimal algorithms) 9 5 (36%) 4 (24%)
META Metaheuristics & evolutionary algorithms 17 10 (71%) 7 (41%)
PRED ML prediction / forecasting models 6 3 (21%) 3 (18%)
DRL (Deep) reinforcement learning 6 1 (7%) 5 (29%)
MAS Multi-agent systems 3 2 (14%) 1 (6%)
DT Digital twin / simulation-based planning 6 2 (14%) 4 (24%)
XAI Explainable AI / transparency 5 1 (7%) 4 (24%)
HUM Human-centric, human-in-the-loop, safety 6 1 (7%) 5 (29%)
LLM Large language models 1 0 (0%) 1 (6%)
Figure 4. Document × tag coverage matrix (P01–P31 in chronological order).

5.2 What the matrix reveals
Two separate groups. The top-left block (STEEL + ENERGY + META/EXACT) is the metallurgical-
optimisation group. The right-hand block (DRL, XAI, HUM, LLM) is dominated by generic job-shop or
process-industry papers. Only P24, P28 and P29 bridge steel + energy + DRL.
Digital twins are used in two different senses: as a physical-model plus simulation layer for furnaces
and rolling (P05, P08, P21, P30), and as a live data layer for RL or human-centric planning (P18, P31).
Uncertainty is mostly handled without learning (fuzzy sets, chance constraints, robust optimisation,
online algorithms, rolling horizons, rule layers, agent auctions) in 8 of the 11 UNC documents. The three
newest energy papers (P24, P28, P29) instead learn uncertainty-aware policies with DRL.
Humans enter late. Before 2023 only P13 addresses user trust. From 2023, XAI for schedules (P15, P19,
P20), safety/intelligence augmentation (P23), LLM with human feedback (P27) and Industry 5.0 fatigue-
aware planning (P31) appear.
5.3 Boundaries of the knowledge domain

—
Implications for the next tasks
Task 2 should test whether the two groups seen in Figure 4 hold up in a content-based network, and
find which documents (likely P24, P28, P29, P18, P13) act as bridges.
Task 3 candidate trade-offs: exact/metaheuristic vs. DRL (optimality guarantees vs. real-time
adaptivity), energy vs. tardiness/throughput, predictive-reactive vs. robust/proactive handling of
uncertainty, and autonomy vs. explainability/human oversight.
Task 4 has to cover the missing combination explicitly: DT + DRL + XAI applied to a steel furnace
is not in the literature we inherited.

Builds on the Task 1 inventory ( extracted/inventory.csv ) — no PDFs re-parsed.
1. Executive summary
Task 1 tagged every document with 12 content markers. Here we turn that flat tag matrix into two structures: a
hierarchical topic tree (a mutually-exclusive primary method plus co-occurring cross-cutting layers) and a
content-based cross-reference network (documents linked when they share two or more specific, non-
generic tags). The network validates and refines the Task 1 hypothesis: the corpus is not one field but a set of
loosely-connected clusters, joined by a handful of bridge documents.

Key findings
Metaheuristics still dominate the primary-method split (13 of 31), but the newest cohort is DRL (6,
five from 2023+) and a small "no dominant method" group (4, all 2023+) made of XAI/human/safety
framework papers with no optimisation core of their own.
ML prediction never stands alone: 6 documents carry the PRED tag but none has it as the
primary method — it is always paired with a metaheuristic or a digital twin.
The network confirms three clusters: a large metaheuristics/furnace-scheduling group, a smaller
"bridge" cluster mixing MAS, exact methods and DRL around uncertainty, and a "trust for
scheduling" cluster (DRL/XAI/META). 8 documents (incl. P09, P16, P18, P23, P26, P31) share no
strong theme with any other single document.
P17 and P28 are the strongest bridges — the two documents whose removal would fragment the
network the most (see §3).
2. Method
"Cross-reference" is built from shared content tags, not citation links: the 31 documents come from disparate
venues and rarely cite one another directly, so a formal citation graph would be nearly empty. Instead, two
documents are linked if they share 2 or more of the 10 specific tags (excluding the near-universal
STEEL/ENERGY context tags) — e.g. both use DRL and both handle UNC. A single shared tag (very common
for META, 17/31) is treated as too weak to count as a link. Each document is also assigned one primary
method tag by priority (DRL > MAS > EXACT > META > PRED) to build the topic tree. Analysis uses
networkx : degree and betweenness centrality (bridge detection) and greedy-modularity community detection.

1. Executive summary
Tasks 1–2 showed what is in the corpus and how it clusters. Task 3 asks a sharper question: on the recurring
sub-topics, where do the 31 documents actually disagree on how to solve the problem? Four divergence axes
stood out: (A) optimality guarantees vs. real-time adaptivity, (B) energy vs. time/cost as the framed objective,
(C) five distinct philosophies for handling uncertainty, and (D) decision autonomy vs. explainability. None of
these are resolved in the literature — each is a design choice Task 4 has to make explicitly.

2. Method
Each document already carries a primary method and a set of cross-cutting tags (Task 1–2). For axes A and D
we score every document on two illustrative 0–1 rubric dimensions derived from those tags (e.g. DRL → high
adaptivity/autonomy, EXACT → high guarantee, XAI/HUM tags → higher explainability) and plot it as a
positioning map — a judgment call made transparent, not a measured benchmark. For axis B we classify the
18 energy-tagged documents by whether their title/keywords also name a competing time/cost objective. For
axis C we read the eleven uncertainty (UNC) documents' own stated mechanism and group them into five
philosophies.
3. Axis A — Optimality guarantee vs. real-time adaptivity

Figure 1. Every document positioned by solution-optimality guarantee (y) and real-time adaptivity (x), coloured by primary method.
The corpus splits into two camps with almost no middle ground, and the top-right quadrant — adaptive and
still guaranteed — is empty. Exact and metaheuristic methods (P04, P07, P10–P12, P17, P22 and the 13-
strong metaheuristics group) solve a snapshot of the problem well but must be re-run, sometimes off-line, when
conditions change. DRL methods (P13, P18, P24, P27–P29) adapt to live state at inference time but offer no
optimality or feasibility guarantee beyond training-time performance. P01's agent-market mechanism and
P03/P06's forecast-plus-robust hybrids sit closest to the gap, hinting at where a bridge would have to be built.
Trade-off for practice: a plant that needs auditable, certifiable schedules (e.g. for safety or contractual
reasons) is steered toward the guaranteed/static camp and must accept slower reaction to disruption; a
plant that faces frequent, hard-to-model disturbances is steered toward DRL and must accept an
unverifiable policy.

A blueprint combining DRL, digital twins and XAI under metallurgical constraints — builds on Tasks 1–

1. Executive summary
Task 3 found four unresolved tensions in the literature and one document-free "target zone": adaptive
scheduling that still carries a guarantee, and autonomous decisions that are still explainable. No single one of
the 31 documents occupies that zone for a steel process. This blueprint is a five-layer architecture designed
specifically to sit there: a digital twin for live state, a hard constraint/safety shield for guarantees, a DRL
agent for real-time adaptivity, an XAI layer for explainability, and a human operator loop for accountability and
trust.

2. Design principles (resolving the four tensions from Task 3)
Guarantee + adaptivity: the DRL agent never acts directly on the plant — every action passes through a
rule-based shield first. The shield, not the learned policy, is what can be certified.
Energy vs. time, stated explicitly: the reward function carries two named terms (energy cost, weighted
tardiness) with weights the plant manager sets and can change — not a single blended score decided by
the modeller.
Uncertainty, combined not chosen: the digital twin's short-horizon forecast and a robust fallback
schedule are always available; the DRL agent is the default, but the shield reverts to the robust schedule
whenever live conditions fall outside the agent's training envelope.
Autonomy paired with explainability, transplanted to steel: the XAI layer used in P13/P19/P20 (built
for generic job-shop/GA problems) is re-applied here to furnace/rolling decisions — the technique exists, it
simply had not been pointed at this domain.

4. Metallurgical & safety constraints enforced by the shield
These are not generic scheduling constraints — they are specific to how steel behaves thermally and how a

in
Temperature window A reheated slab must leave the furnace within a minimum/maximum temperature band
before rolling; too cold needs re-heating (energy waste and delay), too hot damages surface
quality and wastes energy.
P22, P30

charging
Continuous casting and hot rolling must be chained tightly: a slab that cools while waiting
loses the energy already spent on it and may need reheating from scratch.

INTEREST The field just changed — and the old approach has a real cost
The toolbox shifted after 2022. Older studies mostly optimise a fixed plan (metaheuristics); the
newest studies use AI that adapts live to disruptions (deep reinforcement learning) — but that AI cannot
yet guarantee it will respect furnace or safety limits.
Energy savings are usually sold without their real cost. Most studies that target energy treat
delivery deadlines as an afterthought rather than a trade-off leadership actually has to approve.
Explainability exists — just not here. Techniques that let an AI justify its scheduling choices are
mature in other industries; none has been applied to a steel furnace or rolling line.
None of this is hypothetical — it is what a systematic reading of all 31 studies shows, documented in
the accompanying Task 1–3 reports.
DESIRE A system that adapts, stays safe, and explains itself
Task 4 designed a five-layer blueprint that closes the gap above: a live digital twin of the line, a hard
safety shield that enforces metallurgical and safety rules no matter what the AI proposes, an adaptive
scheduler that reacts to disruptions in real time, an explanation layer operators can question, and a
human-in-the-loop override at every step.

The proposed architecture (full detail in the Task 4 report).
Delivered well, this gives the plant real-time responsiveness without giving up auditability — schedules that
adjust to a broken-down line or a late delivery in seconds, while every change stays inside the same safety
and quality rules engineers already trust, and can be explained to the shift supervisor in one sentence.
